Article Title: Why the US is deporting migrants to Liberia instead of their home countries
Article Text:
A plane carrying deportees from the United States arrives at Roberts International Airport, Harbel, near Monrovia, Liberia (Picture credit: Reuters)

Liberia calls arrangement humanitarian

US expands third-country deportation programme

Abrego Garcia case highlights third-country policy

The United States on Thursday carried out its first deportation under an agreement allowing Liberia to accept up to 1,200 people who are not Liberian nationals, marking one of the Trump administration’s largest efforts yet to send deportees to countries other than their own.An initial group of 20 deportees arrived at Roberts International Airport outside Monrovia, according to the news agency Associated Press.The deportees will include nationals from Africa as well as North America, South America and the Caribbean, Liberian information minister Jerolinmek Piah said.Liberian justice minister Natu Oswald Tweh has said those arriving could seek asylum in Liberia if they wished.Piah said the people being sent to Liberia were being received as “guests” and that the arrangement was humanitarian. According to the BBC, he said none of the initial deportees were criminals or facing prosecution in either the US or Liberia.The Liberian government has not disclosed the nationalities of the 20 people who arrived Thursday.Piah said Liberia had “not demanded or received any compensation or promise of rewards” in exchange for agreeing to participate in the programme.He added that the US would provide support to manage the programme and strengthen Liberia's migration system, according to the BBC.Liberia's decision is rooted partly in its history, Piah said, pointing to the country's origins as a settlement for formerly enslaved and freed Black people from the US and the Caribbean.The US State Department declined to answer specific questions about the Liberia agreement but said implementing the Trump administration's immigration policies was a “top priority” and reaffirmed its commitment to ending what it called illegal and mass immigration and strengthening US border security.The Department of Homeland Security declined to confirm Thursday's deportations, citing “operational security reasons”, and referred questions to the State Department.The Liberia arrangement is part of a wider US policy under President Donald Trump of sending some deportees to countries other than their countries of origin.According to the Third Country Deportation Watch, a partnership between Refugees International and Human Rights First that draws on public records requests, news reports and other sources, the Trump administration has reached agreements with at least 35 countries to accept third-country deportees.More than 23,000 people have been deported to 26 countries under such agreements, according to the organisation.The US State Department previously confirmed that Liberia had agreed to accept people who were not from Liberia. However, a six-page agreement reached in September 2025 and published on the department's website does not specify either the number of people to be accepted or their nationalities.Several African countries have also reached similar arrangements with Washington, including Ghana, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Sierra Leone.The Liberia agreement has also drawn attention because of the case of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who was mistakenly deported by the Trump administration to a prison in El Salvador.After being blocked from sending him to his native El Salvador, the administration has said it could deport him to a third country, including Liberia.Abrego Garcia has said he would agree to be sent to Costa Rica, which has said it would accept him. The US government has not sent him there, and he is challenging deportation to Liberia in a federal lawsuit in Maryland.The use of third-country deportations has faced criticism from rights groups, which have raised concerns about migrants being sent to countries where they have no previous connection and where their safety or legal status may be uncertain.The Trump administration has defended the arrangements as lawful.The Liberia agreement is expected to run for a year and could ultimately involve up to 1,200 third-country nationals, making it a significant expansion of Washington's efforts to find alternative destinations for people it seeks to deport.
Article Summary: First group of 20 deportees arrived at Roberts International Airport outside Monrovia. Deportees will include nationals from Africa as well as North America, South America and the Caribbean. Liberian justice minister Natu Oswald Tweh has said those arriving could seek asylum in Liberia if they wished.

Article Title: Ex-Pakistan PM Imran Khan returns to Adiala Jail after medical examination at Islamabad hospital
Article Text:
73-year-old cricket legend facing health issues after 3 years of imprisonment

Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan on Friday returned to Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail shortly after undergoing a medical examination at Shifa Hospital in Islamabad.The development was confirmed to Reuters by a member of his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.The 73-year-old cricket legend has been facing health issues after spending more than three years in prison following his tenure as prime minister.Khan was taken to Shifa Hospital days after the Supreme Court ordered a medical examination. An official from the Shehbaz Sharif-led government said Islamabad was complying with the Supreme Court's order to facilitate his medical examination.Khan's party and family had sought permission for him to remain in hospital.A three-judge Supreme Court panel had ordered authorities two days earlier to take Khan to Shifa International Hospital for a medical examination amid prolonged concerns raised by his family and personal doctors over his health and access to treatment.The court directed that a medical board, including specialists and his personal physician, Faisal Sultan, examine him.The Supreme Court's order came after former Pakistan president Arif Alvi shared Khan's vitals and raised concerns over what he described as "alarming" medical reports.In a post on X, Alvi said, "Imran Khan's medical reports are alarming. I have gone through them with several specialists, and I am writing this in plain language so every Pakistani can understand exactly what is happening."Alvi also highlighted Khan's health concerns, citing his "anxiety and stress levels", "palpitations," and "high blood pressure." He added that while sleeplessness was not mentioned in the report, Khan's medication appeared to suggest the problem.
Article Summary: Imran Khan returned to Adiala Jail after medical examination at Shifa Hospital in Islamabad. Khan, 73, has been facing health issues after spending more than three years in prison following his tenure as prime minister. A three-judge Supreme Court panel had ordered authorities two days earlier to take Khan to Shifa International Hospital for a medical examination.

Article Title: ‘Lindsay Clancy is obviously not guilty’: Candace Owens blames ‘Big Pharma’ for postpartum psychosis as trial nears end
Article Text:
‘Lindsay Clancy is obviously not guilty’: Candace Owens blames ‘Big Pharma’ for postpartum psychosis as trial nears end

Candace Owens says Lindsay Clancy was put into ‘intentional psychosis’

Lindsay Clancy trial focuses on postpartum psychosis and medication

Candace Owens has publicly backed Lindsay Clancy, saying she is “obviously not guilty” in the deaths of her three children. Owens blamed the doctors who treated Clancy and the psychiatric medicines she was prescribed before the January 2023 killings. Her comments have resurfaced while Clancy’s murder trial in Massachusetts is nearing its final stage. Clancy has admitted killing Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, but has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. Her defense says severe postpartum psychosis and the effects of multiple medicines left her unable to understand her actions.A 46-second clip shared by KanekoaTheGreat shows Owens explaining her view of the case. She said she reached that conclusion when Clancy was first arrested and the case became public in 2023.Owens said: “I made my thoughts clear on this the moment that she um was arrested, the moment that it made the news. Lindsey Clancy is obviously not guilty. There are a fleet of doctors who should be imprisoned for what they put her on. I regularly speak out against Big Pharma.”She further added, “They get away with murder all the time and in this case they are getting away with the murder of really her three children but also completely destroyed her life.Lindsey Clancy in my opinion is not guilty. Uh she was put into a an intentional psychosis when she probably just needed to give her kids away for a weekend to get better but they constantly give you these drugs that do not make things better. And the cocktail of 10 pharmaceuticals that she was on is absolute madness. Absolute madness.”Owens therefore places much of the blame on Clancy’s medical treatment. Her comments are an opinion, not a finding by the court. The trial has not established that doctors intentionally caused psychosis in Clancy.Clancy’s defense does not dispute that she caused the deaths of her three children at the family’s Duxbury, Massachusetts, home on January 24, 2023. Instead, her lawyers argue that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis and should not be held criminally responsible.Court evidence has shown that Clancy received 30 prescriptions for 13 psychiatric medicines from several providers before the killings. Her defense has argued that the treatment failed to identify her worsening condition and that the combination of medicines may have made her mental state worse. Prosecutors have challenged parts of that account and argued that Clancy acted deliberately.The case has now reached its final stretch. Testimony ended on Thursday, August 20, with closing arguments expected early next week, according to CBS News. The jury must ultimately decide whether Clancy is legally responsible for the deaths.The case has also brought renewed attention to postpartum psychosis, a rare but serious condition that can involve hallucinations, delusions and major changes in behaviour. In Clancy’s case, experts have disagreed over her mental state and whether it removed her criminal responsibility.Owens’ comments come as the court prepares to hear the final arguments in a trial where the central question is not whether Clancy caused her children’s deaths, but what was happening in her mind when they occurred.
Article Summary: Candace Owens has publicly backed Lindsay Clancy, saying she is ‘obviously not guilty’ in the deaths of her three children. Owens blamed the doctors who treated Clancy and the psychiatric medicines she was prescribed before the January 2023 killings. Her comments have resurfaced while Clancy’s murder trial in Massachusetts is nearing its final stage.

Article Title: Candace Owens calls out Erika Kirk and TPUSA over Tyler Robinson case as accusations of “gaslighting” erupt
Article Text:
Candace Owens (Image via Getty)

Candace Owens faces fresh scrutiny over Erika Kirk and TPUSA claims

Tyler Robinson case remains at center of public dispute

A fresh social media post has reignited the dispute between Candace Owens, Erika Kirk and Turning Point USA over the public narrative surrounding Tyler Robinson ’s case. Grace Ashford shared a screenshot accusing Erika Kirk and TPUSA of attacking critics who question inconsistencies in the case. The post also points to Owens’ latest comments, placing her at the center of another heated debate over the 22-year-old defendant.The controversy began with a post from Grace Ashford, who claimed that Erika Kirk and TPUSA had accused critics of being evil for raising questions about the case. Ashford’s post argues that the public deserves answers when statements made by prominent figures later appear inconsistent with information that emerges.The screenshot features a video of Candace Owens discussing the issue. Owens focuses on a previous statement attributed to Erika Kirk concerning whether Charlie Kirk had been sending text messages shortly before his death.Owens argues that a public correction should follow if new information contradicts an earlier claim. She frames accountability as essential to maintaining public trust, particularly when a case has attracted intense attention online.Owens said:“When Erika publicly stated with confidence on Glenn Beck's show that Charlie was not sending text messages the night before signaling that he was worried. He was going to be killed It then becomes incumbent upon Erika herself to correct the record publicly When we learn that that isn't true. That's how you build goodwill with the public take accountability when it comes to Turning Point USA It's just amazing. It's it feels like we're just being perpetually gaslit by them We're offered a biblical proverb like how dare you even ask us to explain why what we told you before is completely inconsistent With what we're saying now, they're just suggesting that we're evil for noticing these various inconsistencies and illogical points That are being presented by them. ”Her comments have become part of a wider argument over how much information should be accepted at face value while the legal process is still unfolding.Owens then shifted her focus to Robinson’s legal position and the intense public reaction surrounding his case. She questioned why people connected to TPUSA appeared so determined, in her view, to portray Robinson as guilty before a trial has established that conclusion.She also criticized the use of influencers and commentators to discuss courtroom proceedings, arguing that legal filings should be represented accurately rather than selectively.Owens continued:“Why I don't know if it needs reminding but in this country it is innocent until proven guilty So Why does it seem that Turning Point USA and the representatives and their affiliates are so hell-bent on sending a 22 year old young Man to his death. He's up for the death sentence Why are they bringing influencers into the courtroom? Why are they as Blake Neff has done repeatedly completely Misrepresenting court filings to the public in order to do just that To assert that Tyler Robinson is guilty. ""This is a tweet by the way from just this morning from Blakey just Lies and misrepresents and we're the bad guys for noticing that he's doing it. This is what the tweet read. He wrote Utah prosecutors have responded to Tyler Robinson's defense filing ahead of the final preliminary hearing and Confirms what observers pointed out about that filing the defense is very conspicuously not contesting any of the core evidence showing Tyler Robinson committed the murder. ""They don't contest the camera footage the DNA the rifle the cause of death or Tyler's phone data All they have is a complaint about reliable hearsay Which won't apply at the full trial anyway, and then attacks on the aggravating factors If there was any merit at all to any of the theories that Candace and them have pushed the last 11 months Why didn't the defense bring them up? It's stunning to me that he thinks he can get away with this it says Preliminary hearings decide only probable cause under the Utah 1102 standard reliable hearsay is allowed defense counsel often skip alternative theories To avoid previewing their strategy before the trial silence does not prove that those theories lack merit”The remarks highlight the sharp divide surrounding the case. Owens is questioning how Robinson’s defense strategy and court filings are being interpreted publicly, while critics argue that the available evidence should be taken seriously.A key distinction remains important: allegations and arguments made by commentators are not the same as findings by a court. Robinson’s guilt must ultimately be determined through the legal process, and public commentary cannot replace that process.The viral screenshot has therefore become another flashpoint in an already intense dispute. It does not resolve the competing claims, but it shows how deeply divided the public conversation has become around Erika Kirk, TPUSA, Candace Owens and the Tyler Robinson case.As proceedings continue, the evidence presented in court will carry far greater weight than competing narratives on social media. For now, the online battle over what happened, what was said and what the public should believe shows no sign of slowing.
Article Summary: A fresh social media post has reignited the dispute between Candace Owens and Turning Point USA over the public narrative surrounding Tyler Robinson’s case. Grace Ashford shared a screenshot accusing Erika Kirk and TPUSA of attacking critics who question inconsistencies in the case. The post also points to Owens’ latest comments, placing her at the center of another heated debate.

Article Title: What happened to Sonia Bellina? 29-year-old TikTok’s burned body found in French vineyard as two men are arrested
Article Text:
Who was Sonia Bellina and what is her cause of death?

Sonia Bellina death investigation leads to two arrests

Sonia Bellina’s sudden death has left her family and more than 260,000 TikTok followers searching for answers after her body was discovered burned in a French vineyard. The 29-year-old creator had built a following through lip-sync videos and personal content, but her final days have now become the focus of a murder investigation. Two men were detained in connection with the case, although one has since been released.Bellina was a French social media creator known for her TikTok presence, where she had attracted a sizable audience with lip-sync clips and other videos. Her online following made news of her disappearance particularly distressing for fans who had watched her content.According to French prosecutors, Bellina was reported missing on Aug. 10. Two days later, a farm worker discovered a burned body lying between rows of vines in Saint-Gilles, near Nîmes. Investigators later identified the remains as Bellina through DNA testing.Her family had already feared the body belonged to her. Bellina’s relatives told French outlet Midi Libre that personal details, including her breast implants and a ring, appeared to match those of the woman found in the vineyard.The discovery prompted a murder investigation. Authorities scheduled an autopsy, although prosecutors have not publicly released detailed findings about Bellina’s cause or manner of death.The circumstances surrounding her final hours remain unclear, leaving investigators to piece together what happened after she left home.The Nîmes Prosecutor’s Office said two men were arrested because investigators had evidence suggesting their direct or indirect involvement in the incident. However, authorities later confirmed that one of the men had been released from custody.The remaining suspect was kept in detention after prosecutors received an extension through Aug. 21. Authorities said further information would be released after that point.The arrests do not establish guilt. The investigation remains active, and the circumstances surrounding Bellina’s death have yet to be fully established by prosecutors.Bellina’s family has also spoken publicly about the loss. Her sister said during a TikTok live that Bellina had told relatives she was going out one evening but never returned. The family had reportedly been preparing to celebrate her 30th birthday on Sept. 30.Instead, they are now mourning her death while waiting for investigators to determine what happened.Her sister also pushed back against cruel comments appearing online after Bellina’s death. She said some people had posted hurtful claims about the influencer and urged users to stop speculating while the family grieves.The case has drawn attention not only because of Bellina’s online following but also because of the disturbing circumstances in which her body was discovered. For now, investigators are working to establish a clear timeline, determine how Bellina died and understand what led to her remains being left in the vineyard.As the investigation continues, the family’s search for answers remains at the heart of the case. Further updates from French authorities could provide crucial details about the final hours of the TikTok creator’s life and the circumstances behind her death.
Article Summary: Sonia Bellina's body was discovered burned in a French vineyard. The 29-year-old creator had built a following through lip-sync videos and personal content. Two men were detained in connection with the case, although one has since been released.

Article Title: Florida police officer arrested after using Flock surveillance cameras 717 times to track estranged wife
Article Text:
Florida police officer allegedly tracked estranged wife 717 times

Investigators say he entered false reasons

Goodson said he was trying to locate his children

Florida officer faces two charges

Police officer placed on paid administrative leave

What are Flock surveillance cameras?

Privacy concerns surrounding licence-plate readers

A Florida police officer has been arrested after allegedly using his department's Flock licence-plate surveillance system 717 times to track a vehicle belonging to his estranged wife over nearly two years. Christopher Goodson, a 31-year-old officer with the Haines City Police Department, allegedly searched the vehicle's licence plate between September 1, 2024, and June 30, 2026, both while on and off duty, according to an arrest affidavit. Investigators said he used department-issued devices and entered various law-enforcement justifications for the searches, even though his estranged wife was not involved in a criminal investigation. Goodson was charged with official misconduct and an offence involving computer systems and was placed on paid administrative leave. He has also indicated that he plans to resign. The case has also drawn attention to the privacy risks posed by law-enforcement surveillance tools when access is used for personal purposes rather than legitimate investigations.Investigators reviewing Goodson's activity on the Flock system found 717 searches involving the licence plate associated with his estranged wife's vehicle between September 2024 and June 2026.The searches were reportedly carried out using his police credentials and department-issued devices. According to the arrest affidavit, Goodson accessed the system both while working and while off duty. Investigators found particularly high numbers of searches during several months in 2025, including 280 searches in September alone. The repeated searches became the focus of a criminal investigation into whether the officer had improperly used a law-enforcement database for personal purposes.The investigation began after Goodson told a supervisor that he had conducted searches involving his estranged wife's vehicle. According to the affidavit, his wife had told him that The Washington Post had contacted her about an investigation into the alleged tracking. Goodson then reportedly acknowledged that he had used the Flock system to determine the location of his children when they were with their mother. The department subsequently reviewed his Flock activity and found hundreds of searches connected to the vehicle.According to the arrest affidavit, Goodson allegedly selected different law-enforcement justifications when conducting the searches. These included reasons related to wanted persons, drugs and narcotics, criminal motor vehicle offences, assault and battery, fleeing and eluding, traffic infractions, larceny and theft and felony investigations. Investigators reportedly found no evidence that his estranged wife was the subject of a legitimate criminal investigation during the period examined. Her vehicle was also not identified as being connected to a crime that would have justified the searches.The investigation found that Goodson allegedly used department-issued equipment and his employee credentials to access the Flock system. The searches were made both while he was on duty and during periods when he was off duty, according to investigators. This distinction became important because the system is intended to support legitimate police investigations rather than personal matters. The department has said officers are expected to use investigative databases only for authorised law-enforcement purposes.Goodson reportedly told his supervisor that he used the Flock system to keep track of his children when they were staying with their mother. His explanation is included in the investigative record, but authorities allege that the searches were not legitimate law-enforcement queries. The investigation instead focused on whether he had used his official access to obtain information about his estranged wife's vehicle for personal reasons.Goodson was arrested on August 11, 2026, and charged with one count of official misconduct and one count involving unauthorised use of computer systems, networks and electronic devices. Local reports citing the arrest affidavit describe both charges as third-degree felonies. The allegations have not been proven in court, and Goodson is presumed innocent unless and until he is found guilty. Reports also said it was unclear whether he had entered a plea or retained an attorney to comment publicly on the allegations.Following the investigation, the Haines City Police Department placed Goodson on paid administrative leave. He had joined the department in March 2022 and has indicated that he intends to resign. Police Chief Isaac Jackson described the incident as unfortunate and said the department does not tolerate the misuse or unauthorised use of investigative databases. The chief also stressed that police information systems are intended for legitimate official purposes and must be accessed according to department policies and applicable law.The Haines City Police Department has said it will introduce additional quarterly reviews of employees' access to investigative databases. The reviews are intended to identify searches that may not have a legitimate law-enforcement purpose and strengthen accountability around sensitive information. Despite the controversy, the department has indicated that it will continue using Flock technology because officials consider automated licence-plate readers a useful investigative tool when they are used properly.Flock's system consists of automated licence-plate-reader cameras that photograph passing vehicles and use computer vision technology to identify licence plates and other vehicle characteristics. The resulting information can be stored in a searchable database that allows authorised law-enforcement users to look for previous sightings of a vehicle. Police departments can use the technology to investigate stolen vehicles, missing people and other cases. However, the ability to search historical vehicle sightings has also raised concerns about privacy and potential misuse.Goodson's arrest comes amid wider scrutiny of automated licence-plate-reader networks in the US. A Washington Post investigation published in August 2026 identified at least 50 law-enforcement officers who had been accused or charged with misusing licence-plate-reader systems, including cases involving alleged surveillance of romantic partners and former partners. The investigation highlighted concerns about how officers can access large databases containing information about where vehicles have been detected.The controversy centres on the amount of information that automated licence-plate readers can make searchable. A single camera captures a vehicle at a particular location, but a large network can potentially create a detailed record of where that vehicle has been seen over time. Supporters argue that the technology can help police solve crimes more efficiently, while critics say strong safeguards are needed to prevent it from becoming a tool for monitoring people without a legitimate law-enforcement reason.Flock has faced calls to strengthen controls over how police officers use its systems. The Washington Post reported that the company introduced an audit-assistance feature designed to identify potentially suspicious activity, including repeated searches of the same vehicle and searches conducted outside an officer's normal working hours. Such tools are intended to help agencies identify unusual patterns and investigate potential misuse of the system.
Article Summary: Christopher Goodson, a 31-year-old officer with the Haines City Police Department, allegedly searched the vehicle's licence plate between September 1, 2024, and June 30, 2026. Investigators said he used department-issued devices and entered various law-enforcement justifications for the searches, even though his estranged wife was not involved in a criminal investigation. Goodson was charged with official misconduct and an offence involving computer systems.

Article Title: South Korea rejects Trump's claim; estimates Kim Jong Un has 80-120 nuclear weapons
Article Text:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Photo credit: AP

South Korea’s defence minister claimed on Thursday that North Korea possesses around 80 to 120 nuclear weapons, disputing US president Donald Trump’s claim that Pyongyang has 57.The remarks were made by defence minister Ahn Gyu-back during a parliamentary session. According to news agency Reuters, the minister also said Seoul “cannot acknowledge” the 57-warhead estimate and stressed that South Korea cannot develop nuclear weapons or accept US tactical nuclear weapons.The remarks come amid renewed tensions over US-South Korean military drills, which Pyongyang has condemned as provocative.On Wednesday, US president Donald Trump said he planned to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and claimed that Pyongyang had 57 “very powerful nuclear weapons”.“The fact that I get along with him - that's a good thing, not a bad thing. He has 57 very powerful nuclear weapons,” Trump said, adding, “They should have never allowed it. If I were president, I wouldn't have allowed it. But he's got them.”The claim differs from other estimates. In June, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (Sipri) estimated that North Korea had “possibly assembled around 60 warheads, possesses enough fissile material to produce at least 30 more.”Meanwhile, North Korea has repeatedly vowed to strengthen its nuclear force “both in quality and quantity”. Meanwhile, Pyongyang has also denounced joint US-South Korean military drills as provocative.North Korea’s official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) had earlier reported that a ruling party military commission meeting had decided on measures aimed at “bolstering up the nuclear force both in quality and quantity”.Pyongyang has repeatedly described itself as an “irreversible” nuclear state and labelled South Korea its “most hostile” enemy. It has also accused US-Japan-South Korea military cooperation of turning into a nuclear alliance.The statements came as South Korea and the US conducted the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, which began on Monday and are scheduled to end on Friday, six days earlier than originally planned. The exercises were scaled back after Trump ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the 11-day drills, with the move announced by the South Korean and US militaries days later.North Korea, however, said the reduction did not change its view that the exercises were provocative, potentially complicating prospects for an early resumption of diplomacy between Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. It has routinely condemned the exercises.Earlier in April, the International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi had said that North Korea had made a “very serious increase” in its nuclear weapons production capabilities. Grossi had cited increased activity at facilities including the five-megawatt reactor, reprocessing unit and light water reactor at Yongbyon.
Article Summary: Defence minister Ahn Gyu-back said Seoul cannot acknowledge 57-warhead estimate. Remarks come amid renewed tensions over US-South Korean military drills. North Korea has repeatedly vowed to strengthen its nuclear force “both in quality and quantity”

Article Title: Indonesian woman gives birth under torchlight during magnitude 7.7 earthquake
Article Text:
Maria Florida Nogo Kelen gave birth by torchlight during Indonesia’s 7.7 earthquake, naming baby Gempita/Image: Reuters

gempa

A 39-year-old woman gave birth by emergency caesarean section under torchlight after a magnitude-7.7 earthquake cut power to a hospital in eastern Indonesia.Maria Florida Nogo Kelen was eight months pregnant when the earthquake struck East Nusa Tenggara on Saturday. Her complicated pregnancy meant delaying the delivery could have triggered a potentially fatal seizure.Doctors performed the surgery as aftershocks continued and parts of the hospital were damaged.“During the surgery, I was not afraid,” Kelen told Reuters. “I had to be healthy for my kids.”Her obstetrician, Yona Sara Pardede, said the medical team had little choice but to proceed despite the conditions.“As humans we were afraid. The surgery was difficult as she was a small baby. I ask God, please help us. We don't even have a ventilator,” Pardede said.The baby girl was born weighing 1.3kg during the aftershocks. Her mother named her Gempita, derived from, the Indonesian word for earthquake.The premature baby has remained stable in an incubator placed on grass inside a tent in Nagekeo. Kelen suffered a haemorrhage after giving birth but survived.“I was very grateful for the doctors, even when the room had collapsed, they did not abandon us,” she said.The earthquake caused widespread damage across the province. Medical teams have been treating patients in tents outside damaged hospitals, while rescuers have been searching buildings for people trapped beneath rubble.At least 995 aftershocks have been recorded since Saturday, although only 46 were felt. A magnitude-5.9 tremor struck on Monday.The earthquake hit shortly before 6 am at a depth of about 10km, with its epicentre around 68km northwest of Ende on Flores, according to the US Geological Survey.Tsunami warnings were issued after the quake but were later lifted after no significant sea-level changes were recorded.The disaster has killed at least 68 people, injured 135 and damaged more than 1,300 homes, including nearly 250 that were destroyed on Flores. About 5,000 people have moved into temporary shelters, while the provincial governor has declared a 14-day state of emergency.
Article Summary: Maria Florida Nogo Kelen was eight months pregnant when the earthquake struck East Nusa Tenggara on Saturday. Her complicated pregnancy meant delaying the delivery could have triggered a potentially fatal seizure. Doctors performed the surgery as aftershocks continued and parts of the hospital were damaged.

Article Title: Overnight Russian missile strikes leave 6 dead, 33 wounded across Kyiv
Article Text:
A building burns in Kyiv following overnight Russian strikes, as emergency crews respond across the Ukrainian capital. (Photo: @ZelenskyyUa)

At least six people were killed and 33 wounded in Kyiv after Russia launched an overnight missile barrage that damaged residential buildings and public facilities as explosions continued across the capital into Thursday morning.In the Solomianskyi district, the upper two floors of a nine-storey residential building were destroyed, while fires broke out on other floors. People were also trapped inside two residential buildings and a school shelter.The attack struck 12 locations across the Darnytskyi, Sviatoshynskyi and Solomianskyi districts, including a medical facility and an educational institution. Emergency workers rescued people from beneath the debris as the air raid alert continued into the early morning, according to the Associated Press (AP).Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the overnight assault combined ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones, killing 12 people in Kyiv and one more in the surrounding region, while leaving around 40 others injured. He said Ukraine still lacked sufficient anti-ballistic defences and warned that Patriot interceptors remained urgently needed.Russia has stepped up ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv in an effort to strain Ukraine's air-defence stocks.The capital has only a limited number of systems capable of countering such threats.Interceptor missiles for Ukraine's US-made Patriot systems are also in persistently short supply, adding to the pressure on Kyiv's ability to defend against ballistic attacks.US President Donald Trump had previously authorised Ukraine to obtain licences to produce Patriot air-defence systems before reversing the decision.Ukraine has also expanded its long-range strikes deep inside Russia, hitting arms depots, military installations and other strategic targets as part of an effort to erode Moscow's capacity to continue attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Article Summary: At least six people killed and 33 wounded in overnight missile barrage. Blast damaged residential buildings and public facilities across capital. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine still lacked sufficient anti- ballistic defences. Russia has stepped up ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv.

Article Title: US heatwave: Miami hits 100°F record as Oklahoma sizzles at 112°F
Article Text:
Ajogger pushes through the sweltering Miami heatwave, passing a sign holder seeking shade under an umbrella. (Photo: @elnuevoherald)​​​​​

Miami hit 100 degrees fahrenheit on Tuesday for only the second time in more than 130 years of records, tying its all-time high as a heat wave stretched from Texas to the Southeast.The city's only previous 100-degree reading was recorded on July 21, 1942. The latest record also fits into a broader trend of extreme warming linked to human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.Yet Miami's 100-degree record looks modest beside temperature extremes elsewhere in the US. Kingfisher, Oklahoma, reached 112 degrees on Tuesday, a record for August 18, while Oklahoma's all-time state high stands at 120 degrees and Minnesota's at 115. Florida's statewide record is 109 degrees, according to Cable News Network (CNN).Miami's relatively low record is largely a product of its coastal setting. The nearby ocean heats more slowly than land, while regular Atlantic sea breezes typically bring cooler marine air inland and help keep daytime temperatures from reaching the extremes more common in the country's dry interior.This moderating effect weakened on Tuesday, when west winds kept Miami's usual cooling sea breeze from developing along the coast.Drier regions can heat much more sharply, helping explain why the highest temperatures in the US are generally recorded in the desert Southwest rather than the humid Southeast.Miami's high humidity, however, means temperatures do not need to reach desert-like levels to become dangerous. Heat and moisture together can make it harder for the human body to cool itself, increasing the risk of heat-related illness.The city and much of the Southeast have also seen a sharp rise in extreme heat in recent decades. Miami now records 44 more above-normal summer days than it did in the 1970s, according to Climate Central, a US-based climate research group.Miami's average temperature during June, July and August has risen by 2.6 degrees fahrenheit. Climate Central also found that the annual number of days classified as dangerous humid heat — when the maximum wet-bulb temperature reaches at least 77°F — rose from an average of 50 in the 1970s to 117 during 2016-2025.The group estimated that human-caused climate change, largely driven by the burning of fossil fuels, accounted for about 80 of those 117 days.Miami's heat index, which accounts for the effect of humidity on how hot conditions feel, reached 107 degrees on Tuesday. A stalled heat dome, a persistent area of high pressure that traps hot air, drove the wider heat wave, which continued across much of the southern US on Wednesday.Heat advisories covered all of the Florida Peninsula on Wednesday except the Florida Keys, with Miami forecast to reach the mid-to-upper 90s as dangerous heat and humidity persisted.
Article Summary: Miami hit 100 degrees fahrenheit on Tuesday for only the second time in more than 130 years of records. The city's only previous 100-degree reading was recorded on July 21, 1942. The latest record fits into a broader trend of extreme warming linked to human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.

Article Title: 8 on board as twin-engine Cessna charter plane crashes in remote Alaska
Article Text:
8 on board as Cessna charter plane crashes near Alaska radar station

A twin-engine Cessna charter plane carrying eight people crashed Thursday near a remote radar site in western Alaska while flying from Anchorage to Cape Newenham, the National Transportation Safety Board said.The aircraft, operated by Security Aviation, was headed to Cape Newenham, about 40 miles south of Goodnews Bay, according to Clint Johnson, the NTSB’s Alaska chief.The aircraft was carrying two pilots and six passengers, Johnson said.Johnson said the plane crashed on land near Cape Newenham Airport, an Air Force airstrip that provides access to the Long Range Radar Station.The NTSB, Alaska State Troopers and the Rescue Coordination Center were responding to the crash site, he added.The Alaska Rescue Coordination Center said it launched a search-and-rescue operation after receiving a report of an “aircraft incident” near the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site.The centre said further information would be released as it became available but did not respond to questions.
Article Summary: Twin-engine Cessna charter plane carrying eight people crashes near remote radar site. Plane was flying from Anchorage to Cape Newenham, 40 miles south of Goodnews Bay. Aircraft was carrying two pilots and six passengers, NTSB’s Alaska chief said.

Article Title: In 1968, one man left modern life behind, built a remote Alaska cabin himself and spent nearly 30 years living in the wilderness
Article Text:
PC: NPS

Richard Proenneke built his Alaska cabin with hand tools and local wood

Moss, soil and grass gradually transformed the cabin’s roof

PC: NPS

Why Proenneke built his storage cache nine feet above the ground

The overlooked building near the cabin

The cabin and the man behind it

A small site with a larger historical record

Most people notice how much they rely on modern life only when something stops working. A broken heater, an empty fridge or a lost internet connection can quickly turn an ordinary day into an inconvenience. Richard Proenneke chose to live with far fewer conveniences, and he built the place that would become his home accordingly.In the remote Alaskan wilderness, there was no hardware store around the corner when a tool failed or a building needed repair. Proenneke worked with hand tools, local wood and whatever materials he could make useful. His cabin at Upper Twin Lake was small, but almost every part of it reflected careful thought about living alone in a demanding landscape.The story of the cabin is therefore about more than logs and a roof. It is about patience, resourcefulness and the quiet determination to make everyday life work with what is already at hand, there. Every cut, joint and improvised solution carried the practical lessons of someone learning to depend less on convenience and more on his surroundings.Proenneke did not arrive at Twin Lakes with a complete collection of modern equipment.He brought certain steel components for his tools and fashioned wooden handles from material available around him. Much of the work was then done with those basic implements.That approach extended beyond the building itself. When a tool broke, replacing it was not the automatic answer. He repaired it and continued using it. The cabin therefore reflects not just the materials available in the Alaskan bush, but a way of working in which useful objects were kept going for as long as possible.As reported by the National Park Service (NPS), the building is about 12 feet wide and 16 feet long. Its walls are made from peeled spruce logs, with the corners joined through carefully cut saddle notches. It has three windows, each made with thin plastic rather than conventional glass, and a small fireplace constructed from stones gathered locally.The entrance is a handmade Dutch door. Its wooden hinges and lock are among the smaller features that reveal how much attention went into ordinary parts of the structure.The original roof was covered with moss collected from within a short distance of the cabin. It seemed an appropriate material for a home surrounded by forest, but the conditions at Twin Lakes presented a problem.Moss needs considerable moisture to remain healthy. The relatively dry environment meant that it did not thrive as a roof covering in the way Proenneke had hoped. Over the years he kept adding material, eventually producing a thin layer made up of moss, earth and grass.It was not a single finished job so much as something that developed with the cabin. More than 30 years of additions left the roof with a natural-looking covering that became part of the building's character.The cabin was only one part of the small settlement Proenneke created for himself. Eleven feet away stood a raised cache for storing supplies.The structure measured roughly 6 by 4 feet and was made from peeled spruce logs. It rested on poles about nine feet high, considerably taller than the traditional caches commonly found in nearby Athabascan communities. There was a practical reason for the difference. Traditional caches were often situated in populated places, where people and dogs provided some deterrence against wildlife. Proenneke expected to be living alone. Raising the storage structure higher reduced the chances of a bear reaching what was kept inside.A ladder made from local materials provided access. Tin wrapped around the supporting poles served another purpose, making it difficult for smaller animals to climb up. The design was simple, but it showed that the buildings were being shaped around the realities of the landscape rather than simply copied from elsewhere.About 45 feet east of the cabin was a second structure combining a woodshed and an outhouse. Its main section was used for storing tools and keeping a supply of firewood close at hand. Proenneke was careful not to allow his woodpile to run too low, an understandable precaution in a place where heating and cooking depended on what could be gathered and stored.The building followed the basic form of an Adirondack shelter, with a sloping roof. At one end was an outhouse, about 33 inches wide, with a half-moon opening carved into its door. There was a small practical compromise behind its use. Proenneke kept the facility available for visitors rather than having to rebuild or relocate an outhouse repeatedly for their sake. When alone, he generally went into the surrounding woods instead.A home built around self-relianceProenneke's life at the lake was not supported by electricity, running water or a telephone. For roughly 30 years, the cabin remained a place where everyday needs had to be handled without the infrastructure found in ordinary homes.That makes the construction itself more revealing. The cabin was not simply a shelter erected and then left behind. Its maintenance, heating, storage and gradual repairs were all tied to the same self-reliant system.The surrounding site also had paths leading towards the lake, connecting the buildings with the shoreline. From above, the arrangement looks small: a cabin, raised cache and woodshed among the trees. On the ground, each part had a defined purpose.There is another reason Proenneke's cabin remains distinctive. He documented its construction on film. The record provides an unusually direct view of how the building took shape and of the techniques he used. Rather than leaving behind only a finished cabin, Proenneke preserved evidence of the work involved in making it.That documentation also helped give the site a place in the wider story of wilderness life in Alaska. The cabin itself was not the largest or earliest bush cabin in the state. Its significance came from the combination of craftsmanship, self-sufficiency and the record Proenneke left behind.A photograph taken in 1985 shows him sitting in the doorway, dressed in a blue flannel shirt and brown trousers. By then the cabin had already been standing for many years, but it still looked closely connected to the surroundings that had shaped its construction.The cabin and its associated buildings were added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2007. The recognition reflects the site's importance as an example of an Alaskan bush log cabin, as well as Proenneke's role in documenting and communicating ideas about wilderness preservation.The setting matters as much as the buildings. The cabin was made from spruce taken from the area, its storage arrangements were adapted to local wildlife, and its roof changed in response to the climate. Even small decisions were influenced by the conditions around Upper Twin Lake.
Article Summary: Richard Proenneke built his Alaska cabin with hand tools and local wood. Over the years he kept adding material, eventually producing a thin layer made up of moss, earth and grass. More than 30 years of additions left the roof with a natural-looking covering.

Article Title: In 1990, Utah used the world’s largest rotenone treatment on Strawberry Reservoir; over 99% of fish biomass vanished and the rebuilt fishery later produced 715,000 catches a year
Article Text:
Overwhelmed reservoir needed a drastic reset

Military-scale operation across huge watershed

Predatory trout restore the balance

Barriers protect the recovery

In August 1990, Utah wildlife officials carried out one of the largest chemical fish-removal projects in fisheries history, wiping out almost every fish in Utah’s Strawberry Reservoir to save its collapsing ecosystem. The operation, led by the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources (UDWR) and described in publications from the American Fisheries Society and UDWR research reports, removed more than 99 per cent of the lake’s total fish biomass. By clearing out the non-native fish, biologists were able to rebuild the food web and create a healthier sport fishery that later produced more than 715,000 angler catches a year. Located 23 miles east of Heber City, the high-elevation reservoir had long been one of the Intermountain West’s best cold-water fishing destinations. But by the late 1980s, large numbers of introduced Utah chub (Gila atraria) and redside shiners had overwhelmed native game fish. They consumed much of the available plankton and contributed to a major decline in trout numbers.Wildlife managers had already tried a smaller rotenone treatment at the original Strawberry Reservoir in 1961. But when Soldier Creek Dam expanded the reservoir in 1973, increasing its surface area to more than 17,000 acres, illegally introduced Utah chub quickly spread through the newly flooded areas.By 1989, UDWR gill-net surveys showed how serious the problem had become. Non-native forage fish made up more than 90 per cent of the total fish weight in the reservoir. Attempts to stock trout were failing. Millions of hatchery-raised trout fry were either eaten by adult chubs or struggled to find enough food because of competition for tiny aquatic organisms. With the reservoir becoming less productive and fewer people visiting to fish, state biologists concluded that partial netting, commercial fishing and biological controls would not solve the problem. A complete chemical treatment was considered the only practical way to clear the lake.The project required a major logistical effort involving hundreds of people from state and federal agencies. The treatment covered the 17,000-acre reservoir, its many bays and more than 170 miles of streams flowing into the Strawberry River drainage. To reduce the amount of chemical needed and lower costs, water managers first lowered the reservoir to its lowest operating level. Crews then applied rotenone, a plant-based chemical that stops cellular respiration in fish and other gill-breathing organisms and breaks down quickly in sunlight. According to historical American Fisheries Society records, teams used heavy machinery, specialised barges, deep-water pumps, all-terrain vehicles and aircraft to spread thousands of gallons of liquid rotenone and dry powder. Dripper stations were placed along mountain streams to make sure the chemical reached side channels, marshes, springs and beaver ponds connected to the main reservoir. Within days, the treatment moved through the entire system. Millions of Utah chub, redside shiners and other non-native fish died and either washed onto the shore or sank to the lake bottom. Follow-up biological surveys showed that more than 99 per cent of the reservoir’s fish biomass had been removed, leaving the lake with a largely empty food web that could be rebuilt.After the chemical naturally broke down in late autumn 1990, UDWR began a large restocking programme aimed at preventing non-native fish from taking over again. Biologists introduced millions of native Bear Lake cutthroat trout (Oncorhynchus clarki utah) along with sterile rainbow trout. Bear Lake cutthroat were chosen because they become strong fish-eaters as adults. Unlike earlier trout strains used in the reservoir, the cutthroat naturally prey on smaller fish in open water. This gave the lake a permanent predator that could help control any Utah chub that survived the treatment. The plan worked. With less competition for food, the stocked cutthroat grew quickly. By the mid-1990s, fishing records and UDWR surveys showed a major recovery. State fishery data recorded annual catches of up to 715,000 trout during peak years. Strawberry Reservoir regained its reputation as one of Utah’s top trout fisheries, drawing more than one million angler hours each year and generating tens of millions of dollars for the local economy.To protect the recovery, UDWR built permanent fish traps and barriers along important spawning streams, including the Strawberry River and Indian Creek. The structures allow biologists to catch, count and sort spawning fish while preventing non-native species from moving upstream to reproduce. Today, strict fishing rules and slot limits help protect large predatory cutthroat trout, ensuring enough mature fish remain to keep chub numbers under control. The 1990 Strawberry Reservoir treatment remains an important example of modern freshwater management. It showed that large-scale chemical fish removal, combined with carefully planned predator stocking, can restore a heavily damaged aquatic ecosystem.
Article Summary: Non-native Utah chub and redside shiners had overwhelmed native game fish. By clearing out the non-native fish, biologists were able to rebuild the food web and create a healthier sport fishery that later produced more than 715,000 angler catches a year.

Article Title: Billionaire Bill Ackman donates $400 million to brain research: shares heartbreaking story of daughter's coma, says he wants cure, not Nobel Prize winners
Article Text:
Bill Ackman commits $400 million to brain research after daughter's brain hemorrhage

How is Lucy now?

The Ackman Oxman Institute

Billionaire Bill Ackman and his wife, Neri Oxman, announced their new commitment of $400 million to establish a new non-profit institute dedicated to brain research, rehabilitation, recovery and human longevity. The drive for this massive donation came from a tragic incident that shook Ackman. Sharing the heartbreaking story of their daughter's sudden brain hemorrhage, Bill Ackman revealed how he learned more about it and how he decided at that time only that he would make sure that the facilities are available to everyone."At midnight on February 6th, earlier this year, the doorbell to our apartment rang. The doorbell was followed by a pounding on the door. I answered the door and a security person in our building handed me his phone. It was my oldest daughter Eloise. She had found my 26-year-old daughter unconscious on the floor of her apartment and had called 911. The EMT team was already there, but they did not know what was wrong with Lucy or to which hospital they would take her. "This was the beginning of a long journey which started with Lucy being non-responsive because of a massive brain hemorrhage that would need an emergency hemicraniectomy to release the pressure on her brain and remove the blood from the hemorrhage.The operation was successful.Ackman revealed that from Lucy's Oura ring, they found out that the hemorrhage had occurred around 9am, which meant that more than 19 hours had passed from the time of the hemorrhage to the completion of the surgery to release the pressure on her brain.As a father, Ackman told the doctors only one thing: give his daughter the best care possible as he would invest unlimited resources to restore her life, and then he made a promise that he would do that for everyone else.Ackman revealed that Lucy is now in a better place. She was in a coma for several weeks and then was not able to breathe on her own, walk, see, or speak. But now she has recovered her cognition and is able to walk a hundred or more steps. "Each day, she makes a little progress, and daily progress compounds. Every day I tell her that she just needs to make a little progress and it won’t be long before she is back," Ackman said."We remain optimistic that Lucy will return to normal function. It will likely take years, but I believe it is only a matter of time, hard work, and technological progress, along with some, and perhaps a lot, of divine intervention."Ackman revealed that the working name of the proposed institute of The Ackman Oxman Institute for want of a better name. He said he does not want another research center that would produce Nobel winners. He wants it to be patient-centric, to be focused on cures, treatment, devices, and rehabilitation. His company already acquired a 400,000-square-foot biotech facility on West End Avenue between 65th and 66th Streets. Other parcels of land acquisitions are also on track."While the AOI will be a non-profit, it will have highly commercial instincts. The AOI will have its own venture funding and will work to develop innovations to create companies that we will seed, assist, and spinout to ensure technologies, treatments, techniques, and drugs get to patients as promptly as possible," he said.
Article Summary: Billionaire Bill Ackman and his wife, Neri Oxman, announced their new commitment of $400 million to establish a new non-profit institute dedicated to brain research, rehabilitation, recovery and human longevity. The drive for this massive donation came from a tragic incident that shook Ackman. His 26-year-old daughter Lucy suffered a sudden brain hemorrhage.

Article Title: 'I am deeply sorry for the harm caused': Indian-origin hospital CEO takes responsibility for massive drug mix-up at a Nashville hospital during routine surgeries
Article Text:
4 people were given wrong medications at a hospital in Tennessee. The Indian-origin CEO apologized for the error that allegedly left one woman paralyzed

Revelations by local investigation

At least one patient has been left permanently paralyzed after a massive medication mix-up at Ascension Saint Thomas Midtown Hospital in Nashville, Tennessee. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation told CBS News it is actively investigating the mix-up after the Tennessee Healthcare Facilities Commission alerted it to the incident.According to reports, the mix-up took place on August 14 when four patients received doses of potassium instead of standard pain drugs while undergoing joint replacement operations.Dr Shubhada Jagasia, the Indian-origin president and CEO of the hospital, issued a detailed statement taking responsibility for the mishap."Our hearts are with the four patients and their families impacted by this event. On behalf of our leadership and care teams, I am deeply sorry for the harm caused to our patients. We have met directly with each of the families to express our deep support, connected them with spiritual care teams, and ensured they have access to all appropriate resources and ongoing care needed," the statement read.Jagasia noted that the hospital authorities self-reported to state regulators after the mix-up was identified and launched a thorough investigation. "We identified the cause and have implemented corrective safeguards.Our clinical teams are actively using these enhanced safety protocols to ensure the highest level of safety at Midtown," she said adding that the hospital would not reveal the details of the patients and what happened to them.NewsChannel 5 Nashville spoke to a woman who said she was permanently paralyzed from the chest down. She was supposed to have had an epidural for pain but the wrong medication was injected, the report said adding that her family is now speaking with an attorney. WSMV identified the woman as 72-year-old Glenda Dorton.Dorton’s daughter-in-law, Kristina Buell, said Dorton knew something was wrong when she woke up. “She was having a reaction; she was itchy. She said her whole body was burning, and she couldn’t feel her legs,” Buell said.Buell said Dorton is very active and had been putting off the knee replacement surgery because she did not want the downtime that comes with it but the medication mistake changed their lives. “We’re hoping that we can give her the care she needs. This is the rest of her life, and she still has a lot of life to live. So, we’re just hoping to make that as good as possible,” Buell said.
Article Summary: 4 people were given wrong medications at a hospital in Tennessee. The Indian- origin CEO apologized for the error that allegedly left one woman paralyzed. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said it is actively investigating the mix-up after the Tennessee Healthcare Facilities Commission alerted it to the incident.

Article Title: First time in 100 years, North American river otter spotted in the Bronx River: 'I could hardly believe what I was seeing'
Article Text:
North American river otter spotted in the Bronx River after 100 years.

Why did river otters disappear from New York's waterways?

By the early 1990s, river otters became a rare sight in the Bronx section of the Bronx River. Wildlife enthusiasts were jumping in joy when something like a river otter was spotted on camera on June 23. The zoo officials later confirmed that it was indeed a North American river otter making its first appearance after a century in this side of the river."When I first reviewed the images, I could hardly believe what I was seeing," said Hawkins, a graduate of the Miami University of Ohio Advanced Inquiry Program hosted at the Bronx Zoo. "Knowing this may be the first documented river otter in the Bronx in generations was an incredible moment."Hawkins captured the image while conducting long-term camera-trap monitoring of wildlife along the river overseen by the WCS's Bronx-based Education Department. Craig Piper, director of the Bronx Zoo and an interim vice president with WCS's Zoos & Aquarium, called it a "win for both wildlife and people.""There are moments in conservation that remind us why this work matters, and this is one of them," Piper said in a statement."Thanks to a broad coalition of public and private partners, we can celebrate the return of an otter as a result of decades of restoration work to provide cleaner water and healthier habitat."River otters historically inhabited every watershed across New York State, but by the early to mid-20th century, they had vanished entirely from central and western New York, remaining only in remote, protected pockets like the Adirondacks and Catskills.During the 18th, 19th, and early 20th centuries, river otters were heavily trapped for their thick, waterproof fur, which fetched high prices in the commercial fur trade. With no bag limits or closed seasons, populations were rapidly overharvested.As apex predators in aquatic ecosystems, otters are extremely sensitive to water contamination. Industrial discharge, agricultural runoff, and heavy metals (like mercury and PCBs) accumulated up the food chain—a process known as biomagnification. Ingesting contaminated fish caused health issues, organ failure, and widespread sterility among otters.Agricultural land clearing, river damming, and expanding urban development destroyed shoreline vegetation (riparian corridors) and wetlands vital for otter dens and foraging grounds.Spotting of one otter does not indicate big populationIn 2007, beavers returned to the river for the first time in more than 200 years, according to wildlife officials.While researchers caution that a single observation of an otter does not necessarily indicate a resident population, the discovery shows the Bronx River is increasingly capable of supporting native wildlife that has been absent for generations. "This isn't simply the story of one animal. It's the story of an urban river coming back to life," Piper said. "Every improvement in water quality, every acre of restored habitat, every community volunteer who has cared for this river has helped make a moment like this possible. We hope it's the first of many."According to New York's Department of Environmental Conservation, the North American river can be identified by a stout body, short legs, tapered tail, and dense, short, glossy fur. Their eyes, ears, and nose are located atop their heads so they can see, hear, and smell while most of their body remains in the water.Fur color can range from light brown to black, with a lighter, grayish colored chin and throat. Males are generally larger than females, 44 inches and 38 inches, respectively. Body weight ranges from 10 to 30 pounds.
Article Summary: North American river otter spotted in the Bronx River after 100 years. River otters historically inhabited every watershed across New York State. By early to mid-20th century, they had vanished entirely from central and western New York. In 2007, beavers returned to the river for the first time in more than 200 years.

Article Title: 68-year-old Sheila Consaul bought Ohio’s abandoned Fairport Harbor West Lighthouse for $71,010 in 2011, then spent 15 years and over $300,000 restoring it as an off-grid home
Article Text:
Sheila Consaul transformed Ohio’s abandoned Fairport Harbor West Lighthouse into a unique off-grid summer home.

Why Sheila Consaul decided to buy a lighthouse

An abandoned lighthouse in terrible condition

Once abandoned for decades, the Fairport Harbor West Lighthouse now serves as Sheila Consaul’s historic Lake Erie retreat.

She spent more than $300,000 restoring the property

A $71,010 auction purchase became a more than $300,000 restoration project for Sheila Consaul.

She does not own the land

What it is like to live off-grid

The century-old lighthouse combines historic architecture with modern off-grid living, including solar power and rainwater collection.

The lighthouse has a dangerous history

From original hardwood floors to its historic beacon, the restored Fairport Harbor West Lighthouse preserves a century of history.

A lighthouse built to survive Lake Erie

What the lighthouse looked like when keepers lived there

Historic treasures discovered inside

The lantern room and 100-year-old beacon

A weather station and a 360-degree view

Standing on Lake Erie, the lighthouse offers Consaul a 360-degree view

She lives there only during the warmer months

Why she wants to preserve the lighthouse

At 68, Sheila Consaul owns one of America’s most unusual homes, a century-old lighthouse standing in Lake Erie. During a conversation with Tiny House Giant Journey, she opened up about how she went from building a career in Washington, DC, to buying the Fairport Harbor West Lighthouse in Ohio for $71,010 at auction in 2011 and spending more than $300,000 restoring it.What began as an unusual idea for a vacation home eventually became a 15-year restoration project, with Consaul investing more than $300,000 in the property and turning it into a largely off-grid residence while preserving its historic character.Before taking on the lighthouse, Consaul had already restored a historic home, which helped fuel her fascination with old buildings and restoration. While working in Washington, DC, she began looking for a summer home that was historic, unusual and located on the water.The idea of buying a lighthouse sounded fascinating to her after she learned that the federal government was auctioning off historic lighthouses.In 2009, the Fairport Harbor West Lighthouse became available at auction, and Consaul began bidding. It took two years before she finally secured the property, officially taking ownership in 2011. The lighthouse had been built in 1925 and was nearly 3,000 square feet, larger than many of the other lighthouses she had considered.Consaul's winning bid was $71,010. She later used a $200,000 home equity loan to cover the purchase and initial renovation costs, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It.When Consaul first took possession, the lighthouse had been unoccupied since the late 1940s and had fallen into serious disrepair.“There were no utilities, no furniture, no creature comforts of any kind,” she recalled.The windows were broken and boarded up, plaster was falling from the walls and the property was described by Consaul as dreary and sad. The building had also been vandalized during the decades it sat empty. Ohio History Connection notes that the restoration involved repairing original windows, replacing those beyond repair, preserving flooring and carrying out extensive interior and exterior work.Consaul's first night at the lighthouse was far from luxurious.“My first night in the lighthouse was quite a challenge,” she said, recalling how she slept on a sleeping bag on the floor.Consaul estimates that she has spent more than $300,000 renovating the lighthouse, well beyond her initial $200,000 renovation budget.The work included rewiring the building, restoring windows, repairing original floors, painting the interior and exterior and installing systems that would allow her to live there without conventional utilities.The restoration eventually transformed the lighthouse into a roughly 3,000-square-foot property with three bedrooms, three full bathrooms, five levels and four staircases.The project was not completed overnight. Consaul has described the restoration as a years-long process, with work often limited to the warmer months because she only lives at the lighthouse seasonally. A 2026 profile by Fairfax County says she spent 15 years restoring the lighthouse.There is another unusual aspect to Consaul's ownership: she owns the lighthouse structure, but not the land on which it stands.The land belongs to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and Consaul paid $2,500 for a 25-year lease.She has said that as long as she owns the lighthouse, she intends to continue offering private tours. If she is still there when the lease expires, she plans to renew it.For Consaul, owning the building also means accepting responsibility for its place in the local community.“One thing that was very important to me when I bought this lighthouse was that I understood that this was part of this community of Fairport Harbor,” she said.Today, the lighthouse operates largely off-grid.Consaul collects rainwater from the roof and stores it in a cistern. The water then goes through pumping, treatment and chlorination systems before being used in the home.The property also has composting toilets.Electricity comes from sustainable sources including solar power, with a generator available when necessary. Ohio History Connection has also noted the installation of a solar/wind system as part of the property's sustainable power setup.Getting basic supplies is another challenge.The lighthouse has no dock, so Consaul accesses it through Headlands Beach State Park, walking through the dunes and along the breakwater.“People ask me all the time, how do I get supplies here? How do I get groceries? My answer is a backpack,” she said.She explained that the beach is several inches thick and difficult to navigate with a cart, making a backpack easier for carrying supplies in and out.Over the years, friends and volunteers have also helped transport furniture, equipment and renovation materials to the lighthouse.The attraction of lighthouses, Consaul says, comes partly from their history.Lighthouse keepers were responsible for keeping the beacon burning, monitoring marine traffic and helping protect people navigating the waters. Lake Erie and the other Great Lakes can experience sudden and dangerous storms, making the work of lighthouse keepers particularly important.“The mystique comes from the dark of night. Comes from the fog and the wind and the weather,” Consaul said.The remote setting, harsh weather and isolation were all part of the lighthouse-keeper experience.The Fairport Harbor West Lighthouse was constructed in Buffalo, New York, and transported by ship down Lake Erie to northeast Ohio.The structure was built with thick walls, steel plating, steel girders, brick and cast iron. Its beacon was first lit on June 9, 1925, meaning the lighthouse celebrated its 100th anniversary in 2025.The lighthouse was designed to withstand the harsh weather conditions around Lake Erie and was built to last.Three lighthouse keepers lived at the property after it opened in 1925. They worked around the clock to maintain the beacon, initially using kerosene before the lighthouse was electrified in the late 1940s.Once electricity was brought in, the keepers no longer needed to live at the lighthouse and could return to the Coast Guard station on land.The building's current rooms have very different functions from those they had a century ago.The first floor, now a living room, kitchen and dining area, was essentially a working space when the keepers lived there. They used coal for heating and electricity, with coal brought by ship and lifted into the building through a chain winch.The second floor was where the keepers lived. Their families generally remained in Fairport Harbor rather than living at the lighthouse, and the keepers worked shifts before returning to shore.Consaul has also identified what she believes were the original kitchen and pantry areas. The former kitchen contains evidence of a stove and cast-iron sink, while horizontal marks on the walls indicate where pantry shelves once stood.During the restoration, Consaul preserved many original features, including hardwood floors and hexagonal bathroom tiles.She also discovered artifacts connected to the lighthouse's past.One was a crate panel dated May 27, 1943, marked as coming from Frigidaire in Dayton, Ohio. Consaul believes it was associated with a refrigerator shipped to the lighthouse that year.Another discovery was an old ladder marked “USLHS”, referring to the U.S. Lighthouse Service. The service merged with the Coast Guard in 1939, helping date the ladder to before that transition.The original fog horn is also preserved inside the lighthouse.Higher up in the lighthouse is the lantern room, where keepers once serviced the original beacon.Consaul believes a large opening in the room was used to bring in the original Fresnel lens, the large glass-prism lens technology used in historic lighthouse beacons.Today, the lighthouse has a modern LED beacon that remains an active aid to navigation.The beacon is powered by solar energy and comes on every evening at dusk before switching off at dawn. It follows a set pattern of two seconds on and three seconds off.The U.S. Coast Guard continues to maintain the equipment.The top of the lighthouse also houses a National Weather Service weather station, which records information including temperature, wind speed and wind direction.Above the lantern room is the widow's walk, where visitors can walk around the structure and take in a 360-degree view of northeast Ohio.Because the lighthouse sits in the middle of Lake Erie, Consaul is also exploring wind power.“You get a lot of wind,” she said, explaining that she has been looking for equipment strong enough to withstand the area's powerful winds while still generating useful electricity.Despite turning the lighthouse into a comfortable home, Consaul does not live there year-round.Because the property has no conventional heating or air conditioning, she generally spends about four and a half months there.She opens the lighthouse around Memorial Day weekend and usually closes it around Columbus Day weekend.Before winter arrives, she shuts the property down and secures its exterior cast-iron shutters and interior storm windows.“Once October, November comes on, it gets cold and windy and pretty dangerous and icy and snowy and you don't want to be here,” she said.Consaul's restoration has become about more than creating a unique summer home. She sees herself as a temporary steward of a historic landmark.“There are only so many lighthouses left. We are not building more lighthouses,” she said.The Fairport Harbor West Lighthouse remains part of the local community, and Consaul has opened it for annual open houses and private tours.She said one of the most rewarding parts of the project is watching people who have looked at the lighthouse from the shore for decades finally get the chance to see inside.“One of the things I love most about this house is the actual structure. I love living in that history,” she said.After years of restoration, Consaul says she can finally spend more time enjoying the property rather than constantly working on it.For her, the lighthouse is not simply something she bought at auction, it is a piece of history she hopes to pass on.“I’m just a steward of Fairport Harbor West. I hope it will be here another hundred years,” she said.
Article Summary: Sheila Consaul bought the Fairport Harbor West Lighthouse in Ohio for $71,010 at auction in 2011 and spent more than $300,000 restoring it. The lighthouse combines historic architecture with modern off-grid living, including solar power and rainwater collection. Consaul only lives at the lighthouse during the warmer months.

Article Title: In 2020, a catastrophic Michigan dam disaster left Smallwood Lake drawn down; six years and a $50.2 million rebuild later, water is finally returning to 721 waterfront properties
Article Text:
Lake status as of July 21

Work on schedule

Lake refill began on August 4, 2026

Property owners get help

Six years after a catastrophic dam disaster left Smallwood Lake drawn down in Michigan, water is finally returning to the lake. The refill began on August 4, following the completion of a $50.2 million rebuild of Smallwood Dam, and is expected to take eight to 10 weeks, depending on weather conditions. The project will restore the lake for 721 waterfront properties.The refill is an important step in the wider restoration of Michigan's Four Lakes system.
